title: Short Service Life of Cockpit Windshields and Repeat Heating Faults
abstract: Operator reports windshields being removed at roughly half their expected life because of edge delamination and intermittent heating faults, and asks for an improved windshield standard that reduces both the removal rate and the dispatch impact.

sections.request: We are removing cockpit windshields at about half the life we budgeted for. The two failure modes we see are a cloudy band appearing along the bottom edge of the glass, which the crews report as a visibility complaint, and an intermittent heating fault that trips the window heat computer and shows up on the overhead panel. The heating faults are the more expensive of the two because they often happen away from base and we cannot dispatch into known icing without them. Last winter we had four diversions caused by a windshield heat fault appearing in the cruise. The replacement itself is not difficult but the glass is long lead and we are carrying more spares than we would like. We would like a windshield standard that lasts the advertised life and that does not fail intermittently in the heater circuit.
sections.background: Twenty-three windshield removals across a fleet of thirty-one aircraft in the last three years, of which fourteen were for heating faults and nine for edge delamination. The mean time between unscheduled removals is 8600 flight hours against a design expectation of 18000. We have already replaced the terminal block on eleven aircraft under the vendor's own service information with no lasting improvement.
sections.expected_outcome: An improved windshield assembly with a heater termination that survives the design life and an edge seal that resists moisture ingress, available as a direct spare so it can be fitted on removal rather than requiring a fleet campaign, and supported by a revised dispatch position for a single failed heater channel.

type_data.business_justification: Twenty-three unscheduled removals and four winter diversions in three years, against a spares holding the operator considers twice what it should be for a fleet of this size.
